content.thinking:
I'm planning out a Genshin Impact-style alchemist workbench prop: a cel-painted table with gold filigree, glowing potions, tassels, a back hutch shelf, and a stool, sketching rough dimensions for the whole scene before writing the full file in one pass.

Since I can't typecheck this, I'm sticking to simple, well-known API calls—plain objects with a single root joint rather than anything hinged—and planning helper functions for boxes, cylinders, spheres, and lathe shapes to keep the part count manageable while building out all the small repeated details.

I'm also working through colors now, keeping to a modest flat-color palette but leaning heavily on paint-based cel shading for surfaces, since paints don't count against the color limit. I'm sketching out a warm wood-and-gold palette inspired by Genshin's Liyue/Sumeru aesthetic.

Adding wood grain and tabletop plank textures...

Now I'm thinking through texel density across all painted surfaces—estimating total painted area around 30 square meters, which gives a reasonable density, and weighing whether to bump the atlas resolution to 2048 or 4096 for finer cel-shaded edges without the textures getting shrunk down.

I'm also deciding to use flat color strings sparingly, keeping distinct colors under about 40, while relying on cel() paints for most large surfaces to maintain a consistent stylized look. Glowing parts need flat colors since paints can't glow, so I'm planning a cached helper function that maps hex values to shared cel paints to avoid redundant paint objects.

Now I'm starting to lay out the scene's coordinate system, beginning with the table's position and dimensions centered at the origin.

I'm placing four chunky turned legs at the corners with a lower shelf and side stretchers, then designing a front apron with drawers featuring gold handles and teal inlay. The piece faces +Z, with a back hutch panel rising up on the opposite side.

Now I'm detailing the hutch: two upright posts flanking a thin back panel, two shelves (one around mid-height, one near the top), and a gabled crest with carved detailing at the top. For the workbench surface, I'm arranging alchemical props -- a distillation setup with a flask over a flame and coiled tubing leading to a collecting vessel, plus a mortar and pestle and a set of scales.

I'm adding more shelf and floor props: a balance, stacked books, an open grimoire on a stand, a row of potion bottles, hanging herb bundles from the top rail, candles, a glowing teal crystal on a stand, mushrooms, an hourglass, and a cauldron with glowing green liquid on the floor alongside a stool and herb basket, widening the overall footprint. I'm also considering adding a rug beneath the whole setup for extra floor detail.

Now I'm working out the rug geometry: a thin cel-shaded box base with a textured plane on top so the pattern renders correctly, making sure it sits flush with the floor without clipping, since table legs already touch y=0. I'm defining the rug footprint at roughly 3.0 by 1.9 units as the base layer for the group.

Starting the builder code...

Writing helper functions...

I also need to watch for unused variables causing typecheck errors, since I can't verify those until later.

For bottles, I'm thinking through a builder function that constructs the glass body and liquid color, but since true translucency isn't available in this toon material system, I'll fake glass with a pale-tinted solid color and let the liquid color show through.

Instead I'll make the bottle body itself use the liquid color with a glow for magic potions, add a pale glass shoulder and neck, a cork stopper, a gold neck ring, and a thin white highlight stripe decal to sell the glass look, plus a small labeled plane for decoration.

For the lathe profiles, I'm planning outline points starting and ending on the axis so the loop closes cleanly without crossing itself, using enough manual points to avoid smoothing errors on tight profiles and keeping segment counts around 10 with sharper creases below 35°.

I'm sketching out profile coordinates for each bottle type—round flask, tall bottle, triangular vial—then building a generic helper function that assembles the liquid body lathe, glass neck lathe, and cork for any given shape and liquid color.

Still defining profile coordinates...

Still defining bottle profiles...

Still defining vial geometry... Now I'm thinking through glow effects for potion liquids using elemental color palettes (pyro, hydro, anemo, electro, dendro, cryo, geo), and planning glass highlight sweeps as thin white strokes along the bottle body for a shiny look.

Actually, maybe skip highlights and just add a front-facing label instead—a flat plane positioned at the body's surface. But for curved bodies the flat label edges would float away from the sphere surface, looking like a sticker rather than painted-on, so I should consider curving labels to match body shape or just accept the slight gap.

Better approach: use a proper decal projected onto the lathe-generated body surface, keeping all labels facing forward since the decal direction handles orientation. I'll generate label textures as small SVGs—cream rounded rectangle with a colored border and a centered symbol—and project them onto each bottle's surface at the appropriate position and size.

Each bottle needs roughly five parts (body, neck, cork, ring, decal), so with around sixteen bottles that's about eighty parts total, which should be manageable. Now I'm planning the tabletop layout for other items like the balance scale—gold disc base, column, beam, and hanging pans—and figuring out zone placement across the table surface, starting with a distillation setup with tripod and burner on the left side.

I'm placing the burner, flask, swan-neck tube, condenser coil, and collecting flask with specific coordinates, then laying out the center area with an open grimoire on a stand featuring glowing rune pages and a ribbon bookmark, scales at center-right, and a mortar and pestle with herbs plus a stack of books on the right.

I want a candle with melted wax atop the book stack, a small vial rack along the front edge, scattered tools like a funnel, spoon, and dropper, and a glowing floating crystal octahedron on a gold stand with a halo ring near the back-center as the elemental focal point.

Now I'm planning the hutch structure: posts rising from the tabletop to a crested top rail, with two shelves in between holding bottles, books, herb jars, and other collected items at varying heights for a layered, cluttered look.

Then I'm figuring out hanging herb bundles tied beneath the lower shelf's front edge, using small twine-like cylinders and card textures drawn as leafy herb sprigs, planning out colors like lavender purple and chili red for variety.

For these hanging cards I need the artwork oriented so the stems sit at the drawing's bottom and the leafy heads at the top, since the lean-180 flip means the root edge ends up at the top when hung upside-down, pointing the foliage downward naturally. I'm also adding a potted plant on the table using a turned pot shape with soil and outward-flowing leaf cards at varying angles.

Now I'm working out the cauldron prop: a dark lathed iron body with a glowing green liquid disc on top, three leg spikes, a swept handle arc, gold band decals, glowing bubble spheres, and steam card billboards.

Next I'm adding a stool-and-basket set to the side—round cushioned stool, wicker lathe basket with painted stripes and herb cards poking out, plus a squashed sack with a tied neck, positioned near the cauldron.

I'm also considering a hanging lantern off the hutch's right post via an iron bracket, Genshin Liyue-style: red lathe body with gold caps and a tassel card, glowing softly on its chain near x=1.15.

Adding filigree decal planes...

I'm also planning a teal table runner with gold fringe across the center, using mix and smoothstep for staining noise thresholds and a border paint check based on distance from the runner's center.

For the pattern, I'll go with a cheap diamond checker effect using floored x/z coordinates to alternate darker teal tones, skipping actual fringe geometry since it's too costly. For the lower shelf contents, I'll keep things modest: stacked books, a lidded jar, and a small crate with bottles, dropping ideas like skulls or barrels.

Given the scope here, I need to be methodical about setting up imports and helper utilities before diving into placement logic, since writing everything blind risks mistakes. Setting up imports...

Defining wood grain colors and textures...

Adding more palette colors, then I'm sketching a rug paint function with a deep teal-blue base, gold border, and cream pattern using distance-based banding logic to shade the rug's edges.

Adjusting the rug center to (0, 0.1) so it spans properly without overlapping the cauldron or stool positions, and confirming the rug's thin box geometry sits flush on the floor. Now I'm thinking through adding fringe tassels along the short ends using small merged cylinder geometries combined into a single mesh for efficiency.

I'm setting up a geometry-merging helper that attaches the rug pieces to a base joint bone at the origin, then writing a placement utility that translates (and occasionally rotates) geometries before merging them together, keeping rotation order simple by doing rotateY before translate when needed.

Writing fringe geometry...

Now I'm moving on to building the table, starting with the top surface set at y=0.9.

Placing drawer fronts with teal inlay and gold hardware, then working out the leg geometry as turned posts with a profile going from square block through a rounded middle to a shaped foot.

Adding more table details...

I'm also adding an alchemy-themed poster on the panel, like a transmutation circle, positioned between the two shelves where it'll be visible behind the items. I need to check the vertical spacing so pinned notes with wax seals don't get hidden behind bottles on the shelves, and figure out the best placement for the central chart.

Rethinking the hutch layout: shelf1 covers only the left 60%, leaving the right 40% open for a large pinned parchment chart with a transmutation circle and alchemical symbols, plus hanging herbs underneath the left side. Shelf2 then spans the full width above.

Writing bracket geometry...

Adding the crest profile as a wavy arch outline, watching for smoothing issues where sharp corners might cause edges to cross if they're too short for the cut distance.

Placing the crest atop the cornice at the back, I confirm the viewer's sightline to the front table items stays clear. I'm settling on overall proportions now—posts from 0.9 to 1.95 height, cornice box roughly 2.0×0.07×0.18—keeping the whole hutch around 2.2-2.3m tall, a reasonable "real size" for an alchemist's piece.

Now I'm adding details: the cornice sits around y=1.96, with a thin gold trim rod along its front edge, a crest piece near the top, and small gold sphere finials capping the post ends. I'm also starting to position a lantern bracket on the right post.

Next I'm laying out the tabletop surface itself—placing a teal runner mat roughly centered at x=0.1 spanning about a meter wide and half a meter deep, sitting just above the table top at y≈0.904–0.908, which will serve as the base level for items like the grimoire and scales to rest on.

Now I'm designing the distillation zone on the left side of the table, working out the spirit lamp and tripod setup: a small brass burner base with a glowing flame above it, topped by a tripod ring supporting legs that angle down to a wider base, all sized to hold a flask sitting around y=1.05.

I'm then placing a round-bottomed boiling flask above that ring, filled with a glowing violet-pink liquid, working through the proportions so the flask's curve and liquid level sit naturally on the tripod support.

Still working out the swan-neck tube geometry, I'm sketching a curved glass path from the flask's cork upward and arcing over toward the condenser, using a series of control points to define the sweeping shape.

Then I'm adding the condenser itself: a vertical glass tube positioned beside the flask with a teal spiral sweep inside representing coiled water, defined by turns and pitch around the tube's axis.

I'll make the top collar connect to the swan neck tube opening, then route the outflow from the bottom collar down toward the collecting flask, working out the connecting path coordinates for the tube.

I'm repositioning the condenser higher onto a short wooden stand block so the outflow tube can descend naturally into the collecting flask, adjusting the path points to avoid the unphysical upward bend, and setting the flask liquid to cyan.

Actually a pedestal looks odd, so instead I'm building a retort stand: an iron base plate, a thin vertical support pole, and a clamp arm with a gold ring holding the condenser in place, letting the condenser hang free-standing above the flask.

Working out the condenser coil geometry and the connecting tubes—a short outflow path from the condenser collar down to the collecting flask neck, plus a swan-neck tube arcing from the flask over to the condenser top.

Now I'm moving on to the grimoire: placing a wooden lectern-style book stand with a slanted base to hold it.

Settling on 40 degrees for the rotation, confirming the tilted-up normal direction for reading. Now I'm thinking through how to structure the book as a composable function with cover boxes, a page block, and curved pages, positioned and rotated to match the lectern's tilt -- considering whether to use a local coordinate frame or quaternion-based basis vectors to place sub-parts correctly in the tilted space.

Both rotation conventions stay consistent, so I can build a generic part helper taking geometry, color, local position, optional quaternion, and scale. Now I'm working out the local frame for an open book resting on the lectern, rotating the surface normal by 40 degrees about X to figure out how the local axes map onto the tilted rest plane.

Modeling the book as two flat cover boxes, two page blocks layered above them, and a spine piece, then tilting the outer page leaves slightly outward around the local Z axis to create a gentle V shape across the gutter.

For the page artwork, I'm adding textured planes above the page tops: a left page with parchment text and an herb illustration, and a right page showing a transmutation circle with glowing teal lines, keeping the glowing teal strokes on a separate transparent layer so the parchment background itself doesn't glow.

I'll keep the setup simple otherwise -- a red bookmark ribbon, minimal gold rim detailing on the covers, flat stepped pages with a dark gutter line instead of a tilted V-shape, and a small quill-and-inkwell prop near the lectern with a dark glass body and gold lid.

Defining the quill geometry...

Given the huge scope, I'll keep each set piece moderately detailed but compact: next I'm laying out the scales on the runner, starting with a lathed gold pedestal base using a tiered profile, with the column top landing around y=1.248.

Now I'm working out the balance beam geometry — pivoting it near the column top with a slight tilt so one pan sits lower, then hanging the pans from chains at calculated heights below each beam end to reflect the imbalance.

Still shaping the pan geometry...

Now deciding what goes in each pan: the left pan holds a small pile of gold ore nuggets (heavier, sitting lower), while the right pan holds something lighter to balance the scale visually.

For the beam itself, I'm adding a pivot sphere with a small gold spike finial on top, plus a pointer rod descending from the pivot to act as a needle indicator. Beside the scale I'm placing a set of three stepped cylindrical weights in gold and brass tones, and hanging a small gold tassel from the pivot point for decorative flair.

Next I'm moving on to the mortar and pestle piece, working out the lathe profile for the mortar's stone body — shaping the outer curve from the base up to the rim to get a believable carved-stone silhouette.

Still shaping the pestle geometry...

I'm also scattering a handful of flat herb leaves around the mortar on the table, lit from above at a small scale, plus adding a stacked set of books in the back-right with colored covers, cream page blocks, and gold spine trim via a reusable book-building helper.

Still writing book geometry...

Adding gold spine bands and reasoning through spine orientation...

Placing a candle in a holder atop the book stack, with glowing flame details and wax drips, positioned near the open shelf area so it doesn't collide with the chart behind. Now I'm planning a front-row potions rack on the table near the front edge.

I'll color the five vials for pyro, hydro, anemo, electro, and dendro with a 0.8 glow strength, then add two larger potion bottles on the right-front table and a small cluster near front-center with a funnel, dropper bottle, and pouch, leaving the lectern's grimoire area clear.

Now I'm laying out shelf1's contents — a glowing green dendro jar, a row of colored bottles, a line of upright books of varying heights, and small decorative pieces like a jar of cork mushrooms, while skipping anything slime-related.

I'm working out the rotation math for the lying-flat book variant versus the standing one, defining a generic book shape with thickness, height, and depth, then figuring out how to rotate it 90° about the right axes so it transitions from upright (spine +z) to lying flat.

Now I'm defining the geometric parts of the book: the front/back covers as thin boxes, the spine box, and the slightly recessed pages block so the edges peek out from the covers realistically.

I'm also working out the band and title plate details on the spine, then figuring out how origins shift between a book standing upright versus lying flat, plus adding a slight tilt for leaning books on the shelf.

Now I'm setting up shelf2's position and populating it with jars of dried herbs, designing a jar shape with a colored body, pale glass shoulders, and cork lid similar to the potion bottle style.

Then I'm designing the centerpiece: a crystal cradle with a gold lathe stand, a floating glowing octahedron crystal with a vertical gold halo ring, small gems at the base, and flanking elements -- jars to the left, and to the right a scroll bundle with ribbon and wax seal plus a small glass hourglass with gold-capped ends.

Still shaping the hourglass glass profile...

For shelf2 left I'll add a pot with three glowing mushrooms—cream stems with teal half-sphere caps and tiny white spore spots—plus a trio of jars; right side keeps the hourglass, scrolls, and a small bell. I'll skip ceiling-hung extras like dried fish, and add five herb bundles hanging along shelf1's front edge, spaced across the x-range.

Now I'm positioning a drying rail: a thin iron rod running under the shelf, supported by short hanger rods from the shelf brackets, with twine-tied herb bundles dangling down about a quarter unit, checked to clear the table items and distillation bottles below.

For the bundles themselves, I'm setting up card frames oriented upward with a 180-degree lean, using spin/vary/rng jitter to offset positions slightly along x and z so each bundle looks natural. I'm planning six bundle positions cycling through lavender, sage, and flower textures, each built from a few slightly offset frames to create volume.

Thinking through the card orientation: since the drawing's root/tie point sits at the bottom of the texture and the far end at the top, I need to draw stems at the bottom of the image and flower heads at the top, so that once the bundle is hung upside-down, the heads end up pointing downward as intended.

Now I'm shaping the cauldron geometry, lathing a curved profile for the iron pot body with a rounded base, bulging sides, and a flared rim lip, then defining the inner wall offset.

I'm checking the shell outline for self-intersections between the rim lip and inner wall, confirming they stay clear of each other, then sizing the liquid cylinder to sit just inside the vessel wall at the surface height.

Now I'm adding color and glow to the liquid—a green dendro tone with bright small bubbles near the surface—plus wisp cards on top. For the structure, I'm placing three tapered leg spikes angled outward from the body down to the feet, torus ring handles mounted on either side of the rim, and a bail handle arcing over the top connecting both sides.

I'm defining that bail as a thin curved iron rod using a quadratic bezier path, with the control point raised high enough to give it a realistic hanging arc peaking around mid-height. I'm also adding a decorative gold band wrapping around the body near the shoulder, slightly wider than the body radius there, built as a short cylindrical ring with enough segments to look smooth.

For the band I'm matching segment counts between the lathe-generated body and the cylinder band and bumping its radius a touch wider to avoid z-fighting with the belly surface. I'm also planning glowing rune decals applied to the curved front of the cauldron, using a transparent-background texture so only the rune lines themselves emit light, starting with one decal placed facing forward.

Now I'm working out a wooden stirring ladle leaning into the cauldron, positioning a thin rod with a paddle blade running from inside the pot up and out at an angle to look like it's resting mid-stir.

I'm also adding a fire pit beneath the cauldron—a ring of stones with glowing orange flame cones nestled between the legs—but realizing the legs are too short to leave room for fire, so I'm raising the whole body higher to give the flames enough clearance underneath.

Legs placed at 60/180/300 degree azimuths with feet flat on the floor. For the fire, I'm adding three crossed logs under the pot plus layered cone flames—orange outer glow and a smaller hot yellow inner cone—sized to stay clear of the legs and pot bottom. Next I'll set up the right side scene: a stool, basket, and sack near x=1.3.

Now I'm placing the stool with a cylindrical seat, three splayed legs, and a cushion shape on top, then working out the basket's woven profile using a lathe geometry with an inner recess and tapered rim.

Adding basket weave texture...

Now I'm placing a wicker handle arc, then filling the basket with scattered herb sprigs, lavender, and a couple pink flower cards standing upright near the rim, followed by positioning a sack nearby while checking it doesn't collide with the rug edge or stool.

I'm working out positions for the stool, basket, sack, and hanging lantern bracket near the table's right edge and hutch post, making sure nothing overlaps. For the sack I'm shaping it as a scaled sphere with a gathered neck using a cone and tied rope torus, then texturing it with a mottled burlap pattern before moving on to the under-table shelf.

On that lower shelf, I'm populating it with a wooden crate holding corked bottle necks on the left, a metallic bucket with a ladle and rag on the right, and in the middle a pair of lying books alongside a small chest with gold fittings and a half-cylinder lid.

Now I'm placing drawer fronts with handles and a gold nameplate, then working out the hanging lantern: a bracket extending from the post with a diagonal support rod and a small chain down to the lantern itself, which I'm designing lathe-style with gold caps, a red-and-gold striped barrel, and a warm glowing paper-lantern body.

Writing lathe geometry...

For floor details I'll scatter a few leaf cards on the rug and skip coins. Now I'm planning the SVG textures needed: lavender stems with purple buds, sage leaves, dried flower heads, a broad veined leaf for floor/potted plant, a sprig for the basket, the tassel pattern, and 3-4 label variants with cream paper, symbols, and colored bands.

I'm also outlining the remaining decorative textures — ink symbols with accent colors on labels, a teal-and-gold filigree inlay for the drawer front, a pinned parchment chart with a transmutation circle and star polygon, page drawings with glowing teal rune lines, and spiraling wisp textures for the cauldron steam.

Now I'm working out sizing math: setting stroke widths relative to viewBox units so lines stay crisp at different raster sizes, and estimating how many small textures can fit into one shared atlas alongside the larger paint sheet to keep everything efficient.

I'm checking that glow materials work correctly across different part types — cards, rods, and textured parts all need to support glowing meshes, but glow must only apply to flat solid colors, never to paint textures, since that would break the material setup. I'm cataloging the flat color strings used for elemental glow effects like pyro, hydro, anemo, electro, and dendro to make sure each has a distinct shared color string.

Now I'm counting that inventory at around 14 distinct colors, and considering whether small painted ornaments (like tiny gold spheres) can coexist as separate painted parts without conflicting with the flat-color glow system. With roughly 600 painted parts each needing their own UV rectangle in a shared paint sheet, I'm thinking through how the texel interpolation across triangles would work for baking this efficiently.

Tallying up part counts across all the objects—table, hutch, bottles, books, distillation setup, scales, cauldron, lantern, herbs, rug—I land around 600 total, comfortably under the 1000 limit, with merging strategies planned for fringe and bolts. Now I'm starting to write the actual implementation code.

Setting up imports...

Still defining shape helpers...

Still building the local frame helper...

I'm working out how a local sub-rotation combines with the parent quaternion, and verifying the math for orienting a plane to face local +Y by rotating -90° about X—confirming the z-axis maps correctly to the y-axis so the texture plane lies flat like a book page.

Then I'm checking the reading orientation: whether the top of the drawn text ends up pointing toward local -Z (so it reads correctly up the lectern's slope), and after applying the lectern's 40° tilt, confirming the drawing's top faces up and back as expected. I'm also double-checking the viewer's perspective from +Z looking toward -Z, worried that the plane's +X axis might appear mirrored (left instead of right) from that viewpoint, and reasoning through how a +Y-facing plane with its top oriented toward -Z would actually look to someone viewing it from above and in front.

Confirmed unmirrored for the vertical plane too. For textured parts, I should default to the same +Z-facing orientation unless a direction override is given, and when a texture has colored userData, the part's own color should default to white so the texture's original colors show through unaltered.

I'm also handling z-fighting by offsetting coincident planes (drawer fronts, page overlays) by a couple millimeters, and now I'm setting up the shape definitions for the bottle generator, mapping each shape type (round, tall, tri, vial, jar) to its body/neck outline functions and dimensions. Defining shape functions...

Still defining bottle shape coordinates...

The vial's too thin with that radius, so I'm reworking the proportions, targeting roughly 0.12m height with a 0.02m radius for realistic glassware scale, adjusting the body and neck coordinates accordingly.

For the jar shape, I'm defining the body profile with a slight shoulder taper, a short neck for a glass shoulder, and switching the cap to a gold lid instead of cork. Now I'm writing the potion helper function that lathes the shape geometry with configurable glow, labels, cork/lid styling, and ring details.

I need to make sure glow only applies when the liquid is a flat color string rather than a cel-shaded paint object, since the Part type passed to glow needs a mesh property that matches. I'm also considering whether a flatly glowing opaque body loses too much shading like in Genshin-style potions, so I might add a highlight stripe or bubbles to preserve form.

Writing cork and seal geometry...

Now I'm adding a small white highlight sphere to the body to simulate a light reflection, positioning it toward the front-left and adjusting its offset depending on whether the body shape is a sphere or a tri-based form, since the sloped surface needs a different placement to sit flush.

I'm adding decal placement for labels on round/tall/jar shapes, positioned near the front surface, and sketching out an SVG label texture with accent colors and symbols.

Still writing SVG code...

Still writing book parts...

Still placing gold bands and spine details, then adding a title plate and considering gold corner nubs on the front cover corners away from the spine.

I'm limiting corner decorations to flagship books only to keep cost down, skipping clasps for now, and estimating about 8 decoration parts per book. For lying books I'm adding a gold emblem decal on the visible top board face, adjusting the plane orientation for the rotated local frame.

Writing wood plank shader logic...

Defining more wood paint variants...

I'm thinking about the overall palette now: leaning Genshin Liyue-inspired with warm lacquered wood, gold trim, and a teal-painted hutch back panel to give strong contrast behind displayed items like bottles.

Adding a diamond lattice pattern on the panel with subtle darker teal lines, placing the pin chart on it, then moving to define the table's apron, drawer, top, and leg woods before working on the rug paint.

Refining the rug pattern with an elliptical radial coordinate to create concentric medallion rings in gold, deep blue, and cream...

I'm checking the lighting calculation confirms the surface is lit, then moving on to the runner paint function, which defines a border pattern with gold and teal edges around a box roughly 1.0 wide and 0.52 deep.

Now I'm laying out the tabletop positions carefully so nothing overlaps—placing the distillation stand's lamp, flask, pole, condenser, and collecting flask along the x-axis with specific coordinates, making sure the collecting flask sits just before where the runner begins.

I notice the swan neck tube connecting the flask to the condenser would cross right through the pole at the same depth, so I'm nudging the pole forward in z to avoid the collision.

Adding a ring clamp cylinder around the condenser at that same point. Now I'm checking the scale position between the two pans, and verifying the grimoire lectern doesn't collide with the pans given its tilt and height, computing the lectern's top rear point against the pan positions.

Still, there's a slight overlap, so I'm shifting the lectern further left and adjusting the scale's center position so the pans sit at new x-coordinates, then checking those against the mortar and pestle placement — confirming the pans clear the mortar top since they sit higher, and the pestle's lean also stays clear. I'm now considering nudging the mortar's position too, to clean up the remaining minor overlap.

I'm working out the lectern geometry: a base plate, two triangular side cheeks forming the slanted support, and the angled reading surface on top, calculating the ~32° slope angle needed so the rest rises properly over its depth, while checking how it sits relative to the table runner.

I need to fix the extrusion direction so the outline's forward axis actually points toward +z, then position it centered at the right height with the correct thickness of 0.018. For the rest surface, I'm computing the plane through the two edge heights and offsetting the center plane up by half the board thickness of 0.012.

I need to reconsider the origin point — placing it at the hypotenuse surface itself rather than offset, then adding the board's half-thickness (0.006) along the normal so its bottom rests flush: O=(−0.12, 1.0505+0.012·cos32, 0.12+0.012·sin32)≈(−0.12, 1.0607, 0.1264).

Now I'm laying out the front lip ledge to hold the book in place, then building the open book itself: purple cover halves on either side of a thin spine strip, with page blocks sized to fit between them to form the spread.

For the page tops I'm adding thin leaf boxes tilted slightly upward toward the center, rotating each half around the vertical axis by a small angle so the pages appear to curve naturally into the spine.

I'm deciding to simplify and skip the page tilt quaternion math entirely — flat stepped pages with a dark central gutter strip will look fine and save complexity. Now I'm placing the page planes themselves, starting with the left page position, rotation, and size.

I'm building the ribbon with three rod segments for the gutter line and droop, plus a tasseled end with a gold bead. Then I'm placing the inkwell and quill near the lectern, positioning them between the collecting flask and potion tray so nothing overlaps, before moving on to the weights.

Now I'm laying out the cylindrical weights near the scales, placing a pouch with a tassel at the lectern's front ledge, and arranging the big bottles and mortar off to the front right with distinct radii and labels for pyro and hydro types.

Checking distances between the mortar and the round bottle reveals an overlap, so I'm shifting the mortar further right and down, repositioning the tall and triangular bottles to clear space, and confirming the candle stack height stays below the mortar's base so nothing collides.

Now I'm filling in the open table areas: adding a potted plant near the back-right with enough vertical clearance under the shelf, and checking the back-left region under the shelf for space to place a small row of items like a ceramic pot, ladle, and spare bottles without exceeding the shelf's height limit.

Then I consider placement behind the lectern — some bottles and a jar there will be partially hidden by the lectern top, which is fine since they're background items. I also note the hutch posts and table's back edge for spacing, and think about hanging herb bundles from the shelf rail, sizing them so they don't droop too far down.

There's a conflict though: the hanging herbs overlap in depth with the back-row bottles on the table. I decide to shift the herb rail slightly forward and restrict the back-table items to the right side only, keeping the left region under shelf1 clear except for the hanging herbs and the lectern in front.

Adding a low teal-glazed ceramic crock at the table's back-middle keeps that spot filled without height conflicts. I'm placing herb bundles along the rail at even intervals, checking that hanging bottoms and flask necks clear the shelf above, then moving on to work out the layout of the hutch on the left.

Shelf1 spans the left post out to a free right end held by two brackets plus a middle one, with a gold trim rod along the front edge; shelf2 runs the full width above it, supported by brackets at both ends. I'm placing a poster chart on the right wall sized and positioned to sit cleanly within that shelf span.
